thaat: Bilawal (by parentage, though technically from Carnatic tradition)
time_of_day: Night — anytime after 9pm; also used at concerts at any time
aaroh: Sa Re Ga Pa Ni Sa (Ma and Dha omitted)
avaroh: Sa Ni Pa Ga Re Sa
notes_used: Sa, Re shuddh, Ga shuddh, Pa shuddh, Ni shuddh — only 5 shuddh notes; Ma and Dha absent
characteristic_pakad: Ga Pa Ni Sa, Ni Pa Ga Re Sa
emotional_resonance: need for clarity and brightness at night
feeling clouded or foggy in the evening
winding down after a busy day without sadness
a light, clean closing to the day
wanting to meditate with a light, clear mind
after completing something good — a sense of clean satisfaction
wanting simplicity in the evening without the weight of deeper raags
therapy_note: Hansdhwani is one of the most beloved raags for its sheer beauty and simplicity — it sounds like a swan (hans) gliding on still water. Like Bhoopali it is pentatonic, but its notes (including Ni) give it a brighter, slightly more elevated quality compared to Bhoopali's more grounded earthiness. It creates instant calm and clarity — it is the raag of the clear, untroubled mind.

bollywood_references.title: Vatapi Ganapathim (classical Carnatic composition)
bollywood_references.note: This Carnatic composition in Hamsadhvani is the most famous piece in this raag

classical_reference: Originally a Carnatic raag (Hamsadhvani) adopted into Hindustani. M.S. Subbulakshmi's 'Vatapi Ganapathim' is the universal reference. In Hindustani, Pandit Ravi Shankar popularized it on sitar.
notes_for_vocalist: Ma and Dha are strictly absent — if either appears, it is no longer Hansdhwani. The Ni shuddh at the top of the scale creates brightness — this is what distinguishes it from Bhoopali (which has Dha instead of Ni). The Ga-Pa-Ni movement is the heart of the raag. This is an accessible raag for singers of all levels — its purity makes it forgiving and beautiful.
